claim: COPI-coated vesicles originate at the Golgi or endosomes, and mediate retrograde transport to early Golgi cisternae or back to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: COPI-coated vesicles originate at the Golgi or endosomes, and mediate retrograde transport to early Golgi cisternae or back to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Bonifacino and Glick, 2004; Letourneur et al., 1994; Tojima et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Bonifacino and Glick, 2004; Letourneur et al., 1994; Tojima et al., 2019).

claim: COPI is a highly conserved heptameric protein complex consisting of α, β, β', γ, δ, ε, and ζ subunits.
source: COPI is a highly conserved heptameric protein complex (α, β, β', γ, δ, ε, and ζ subunits) that is recruited to Golgi membranes by the small GTP-binding protein Arf (Arf1 and Arf2 in budding yeast) (Hsu, 2011; Serafini et al., 1991; Thomas and Fromme, 2020; Waters et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Hsu, 2011; Serafini et al., 1991; Thomas and Fromme, 2020; Waters et al., 1991).

claim: COPI is recruited to Golgi membranes by the small GTP-binding protein Arf (Arf1 and Arf2 in budding yeast).
source: COPI is a highly conserved heptameric protein complex (α, β, β', γ, δ, ε, and ζ subunits) that is recruited to Golgi membranes by the small GTP-binding protein Arf (Arf1 and Arf2 in budding yeast) (Hsu, 2011; Serafini et al., 1991; Thomas and Fromme, 2020; Waters et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Hsu, 2011; Serafini et al., 1991; Thomas and Fromme, 2020; Waters et al., 1991).

claim: The N-terminal WD repeat (WDR) domains of α- and β′-COP recognize sorting signals on cargoes, such as dilysine motifs (KKxx and KxKxx) commonly found at the C-terminus of ER-resident membrane proteins.
source: The N-terminal WD repeat (WDR) domains of α- and β′-COP recognize sorting signals on cargoes, such as dilysine motifs (KKxx and KxKxx) commonly found at the C-terminus of ER-resident membrane proteins (Eugster et al., 2004; Jackson et al., 2012; Ma and Goldberg, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Eugster et al., 2004; Jackson et al., 2012; Ma and Goldberg, 2013).

claim: Mutations that impair the ability of both α- and β′-COP to bind dilysine motifs disrupt trafficking of well-studied dilysine cargoes, but these mutations do not affect cell viability.
source: Mutations that impair the ability of both α- and β′-COP to bind dilysine motifs disrupt trafficking of well-studied dilysine cargoes, but these mutations do not affect cell viability (Jackson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Jackson et al., 2012).

claim: COPI is essential in yeast and cells are unviable when both terminal propeller domains of α- and β′-COP are deleted.
source: However, COPI is essential in yeast and cells are unviable when both terminal propeller domains of α- and β′-COP are deleted (Eugster et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Eugster et al., 2004).

claim: Important but poorly understood mechanisms exist for COPI recognition of cargoes lacking dilysine motifs.
source: These observations imply that important but poorly understood mechanisms exist for COPI recognition of cargoes lacking dilysine motifs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that COPI is essential despite dilysine binding not being essential for viability.

claim: SNAREs are essential for vesicle fusion with the target membrane and are proposed to prime, or nucleate, coat formation.
source: SNAREs are another critical cargo of COPI vesicles because they are essential for vesicle fusion with the target membrane and are proposed to prime, or nucleate, coat formation (Chen and Scheller, 2001; Rein et al., 2002; Rothman and Warren, 1994; Springer et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Chen and Scheller, 2001; Rein et al., 2002; Rothman and Warren, 1994; Springer et al., 1999).

claim: Few sorting signals have been identified in SNARE proteins and how they are incorporated into COPI vesicles is incompletely understood.
source: Few sorting signals have been identified in SNARE proteins and how they are incorporated into COPI vesicles is incompletely understood (Black and Pelham, 2000; Daste et al., 2013; Fukasawa et al., 2004; Gao and Banfield, 2020; Jackson et al., 2010; Mancias and Goldberg, 2007; Martinez-Arca et al., 2003; Miller et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Black and Pelham, 2000; Daste et al., 2013; Fukasawa et al., 2004; Gao and Banfield, 2020; Jackson et al., 2010; Mancias and Goldberg, 2007; Martinez-Arca et al., 2003; Miller et al., 2007).

claim: The ArfGAP protein Glo3 interacts with COPI, Arf-GTP, and SNAREs and is proposed to be part of the priming complex.
source: The ArfGAP protein Glo3 may contribute to SNARE localization because it is known to interact with COPI, Arf-GTP, and SNAREs and is proposed to be part of the priming complex (Rein et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Rein et al., 2002).

claim: Glo3 stimulates conversion of Arf-GTP to Arf-GDP, which destabilizes the COPI coat and is crucial for vesicle uncoating.
source: In addition, Glo3 stimulates conversion of Arf-GTP to Arf-GDP, which destabilizes the COPI coat and is crucial for vesicle uncoating (Tanigawa et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Tanigawa et al., 1993).

claim: COPI plays a role in the recycling of a budding yeast v-SNARE, Snc1, from the endocytic pathway to the trans-Golgi network (TGN) through recognition of a polyubiquitin (polyUb) signal.
source: We recently found that COPI plays a role in the recycling of a budding yeast v-SNARE, Snc1, from the endocytic pathway to the trans-Golgi network (TGN) through recognition of a polyubiquitin (polyUb) signal (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Xu et al., 2017).

claim: The cargo-binding WDR domains of α-COP and β′-COP bind specifically to polyUb.
source: The cargo-binding WDR domains of α-COP and β′-COP bind specifically to polyUb (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Xu et al., 2017).

claim: Deletion of the β′-COP N-terminal WDR domain (β′-COP ∆2–304) disrupts Snc1 recycling.
source: Deletion of the β′-COP N-terminal WDR domain (β′-COP ∆2–304) disrupts Snc1 recycling while the replacement of this domain with unrelated ubiquitin-binding domains (UBDs) restores Snc1 recycling.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Xu et al., 2017).

claim: Replacement of the β′-COP N-terminal WDR domain with unrelated ubiquitin-binding domains (UBDs) restores Snc1 recycling.
source: Deletion of the β′-COP N-terminal WDR domain (β′-COP ∆2–304) disrupts Snc1 recycling while the replacement of this domain with unrelated ubiquitin-binding domains (UBDs) restores Snc1 recycling.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Xu et al., 2017).

claim: The β′-COP ∆2–304 mutant displays a slow growth phenotype, which is fully corrected by addition of an unrelated UBD.
source: In addition, the β′-COP ∆2–304 mutant displays a slow growth phenotype, which is fully corrected by addition of the unrelated UBD.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Xu et al., 2017).

claim: β′-COP–UBD fusion proteins are incapable of binding dilysine motifs.
source: Because the β′-COP–UBD fusion proteins are incapable of binding dilysine motifs, these observations suggest a direct role for COPI–Ub interaction in Snc1 recycling (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Xu et al., 2017).

claim: The COPI–ubiquitin interaction plays a direct role in Snc1 recycling.
source: Because the β′-COP–UBD fusion proteins are incapable of binding dilysine motifs, these observations suggest a direct role for COPI–Ub interaction in Snc1 recycling (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that UBD fusion proteins that cannot bind dilysine motifs can still support Snc1 recycling.

claim: Emp47 is the only other cargo known to be missorted in the β′-COP ∆2–304 mutant besides Snc1.
source: The only other cargo known to be missorted in the β′-COP ∆2–304 mutant is Emp47, which bears a variant dilysine motif (KxKxx) that is uniquely recognized by the β′ propeller domain and the trafficking of Emp47 does not require ubiquitin interaction (Eugster et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Eugster et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2017).

claim: Emp47 bears a variant dilysine motif (KxKxx) that is uniquely recognized by the β′ propeller domain.
source: The only other cargo known to be missorted in the β′-COP ∆2–304 mutant is Emp47, which bears a variant dilysine motif (KxKxx) that is uniquely recognized by the β′ propeller domain and the trafficking of Emp47 does not require ubiquitin interaction (Eugster et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Eugster et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2017).

claim: The trafficking of Emp47 does not require ubiquitin interaction.
source: The only other cargo known to be missorted in the β′-COP ∆2–304 mutant is Emp47, which bears a variant dilysine motif (KxKxx) that is uniquely recognized by the β′ propeller domain and the trafficking of Emp47 does not require ubiquitin interaction (Eugster et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Eugster et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2017).

claim: Rer1-GFP is sorted normally by β′-COP ∆2–304.
source: Another COPI cargo analyzed, Rer1-GFP, is sorted normally by β′-COP ∆2–304 (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Xu et al., 2017).

claim: The normal localization of several SNAREs functioning at the ER–Golgi interface or within the Golgi, including Bet1, Gos1, Snc2, Bos1, and Sec22, requires COPI–ubiquitin interactions.
source: We show that the normal localization of several SNAREs functioning at the ER–Golgi interface or within the Golgi, including Bet1, Gos1, Snc2, Bos1, and Sec22, requires COPI–ubiquitin interactions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing mislocalization of these SNAREs in β′-COP ∆2–304 mutant.

claim: Several Golgi SNAREs, COPI subunits, and the ArfGAP Glo3 are ubiquitinated under physiological conditions in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: In addition, several Golgi SNAREs, COPI subunits, and the ArfGAP Glo3 are ubiquitinated under physiological conditions in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing ubiquitination of these components.

claim: Ubiquitination of COPI and SNARE components strengthens the interaction between Golgi SNAREs and COPI.
source: Importantly, we show that ubiquitination of these components strengthens the interaction between Golgi SNAREs and COPI while apparently excluding Glo3, providing critical new mechanistic insight into priming mechanisms for COPI vesicle formation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing enhanced COPI-SNARE interactions under ubiquitin-preserved conditions.

claim: Ubiquitination of COPI and SNARE components apparently excludes Glo3 from the SNARE-COPI complex.
source: Importantly, we show that ubiquitination of these components strengthens the interaction between Golgi SNAREs and COPI while apparently excluding Glo3, providing critical new mechanistic insight into priming mechanisms for COPI vesicle formation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing that Glo3 is not enriched in ubiquitin-stabilized SNARE-COPI complexes.

claim: Bet1, Gos1, Snc1, and Snc2 accumulate in elongated tube- and ring-like structures in β′-COP ∆2–304 cells.
source: However, for Bet1, Gos1, Snc1, and Snc2, a significant accumulation of individual SNAREs to elongated tube- and ring-like structures was observed in β′-COP ∆2–304 (Figure 1b, c).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1b, c.

claim: Bet1 and Snc2 were found in ring- and tube-shaped structures while Gos1 was rarely observed in the rings.
source: Bet1 and Snc2 were found in ring- and tube-shaped structures while Gos1 was rarely observed in the rings.
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Snc2 plasma membrane localization was reduced in the β′-COP ∆2–304 mutant.
source: As previously shown for Snc1 (Xu et al., 2017), Snc2 plasma membrane localization was also reduced in the COPI mutant.
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data presented in the manuscript and citation to prior work (Xu et al., 2017).

claim: Tlg1 localized to enlarged tubular structures in β′-COP ∆2–304 cells.
source: Tlg1 also localized to enlarged tubular structures and Snc1 colocalizes to these enlarged structures in the β′-COP ∆2–304 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a; Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Snc1 colocalizes to enlarged tubular structures with Tlg1 in β′-COP ∆2–304 cells.
source: Tlg1 also localized to enlarged tubular structures and Snc1 colocalizes to these enlarged structures in the β′-COP ∆2–304 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a; Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and citation to prior work (Xu et al., 2017).

claim: Sec22 and Bos1 were partially mislocalized to vacuolar structures in β′-COP ∆2–304 cells.
source: In addition, Sec22 and Bos1 were partially mislocalized to vacuolar structures in β′-COP ∆2–304 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: 40% of the GFP-Sec22 chimera was cleaved in β′-COP ∆2–304 cells to release free GFP, in contrast to WT cells where less than 5% was cleaved.
source: Consistently, immunoblotting of cell lysates with anti-GFP indicated that 40% of the GFP-Sec22 chimera was cleaved in β′-COP ∆2–304 cells to release free GFP, in contrast to WT cells where less than 5% was cleaved (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c, d).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c, d.

claim: Comparable morphological changes were observed with Bet1, Snc1, and Snc2 localizing to elongated tubular- and ring-like structures in β′-COP ∆2–304 relative to WT cells when expressed using the weaker, inducible CUP1 promoter.
source: Comparable morphological changes were observed with these SNAREs localizing to elongated tubular- and ring-like structures in β′-COP ∆2–304 relative to WT cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a, b).
evidence: Supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a, b.

claim: Bet1 and Gos1 display an unusual mislocalization phenotype from normal punctate Golgi in WT cells to abnormal tubular and ring-shaped structures that lack Golgi markers in β′-COP ∆2–304 cells.
source: Bet1 and Gos1, however, display an unusual mislocalization phenotype from normal punctate Golgi in WT cells to abnormal tubular and ring-shaped structures that lack Golgi markers in β′-COP ∆2–304 cells.
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: mNG-Gos1 colocalized substantially with Chs5, Sec7, and Mnn9 in WT cells but showed a significant decrease in colocalization with these markers in β′-COP ∆2–304 cells.
source: mNG-Gos1 colocalized substantially with Chs5, Sec7, and Mnn9 in WT cells but showed a significant decrease in colocalization with these markers in in β′-COP ∆2–304 cells.
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis data shown in Figure 2a, b.

claim: Gos1 weakly colocalized with Anp1 in WT cells and this overlap was also diminished in β′-COP ∆2–304.
source: Gos1 weakly colocalized with Anp1 in WT cells and this overlap was also diminished in β′-COP ∆2–304 (Figure 2a, b).
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis data shown in Figure 2a, b.

claim: mNG-Bet1 showed a significant reduction in colocalization with all four Golgi markers (Anp1, Mnn9, Chs5, and Sec7) in β′-COP ∆2–304.
source: mNG-Bet1 also showed a significant reduction in colocalization with all four Golgi markers in β′-COP ∆2–304 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, b).
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, b.

claim: Bet1 colocalized with the medial-Golgi marker Aur1 in WT cells and the degree of this colocalization was reduced in β′-COP ∆2–304.
source: We also observed colocalization of Bet1 with the medial-Golgi marker Aur1 in WT cells and the degree of this colocalization was also reduced in β′-COP ∆2–304 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, b).
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a, b.

claim: There was no noticeable difference in Anp1, Mnn9, Chs5, or Sec7 localization or the morphology of the Golgi compartments these proteins marked in β′-COP ∆2–304 cells compared to WT cells.
source: In addition, there was no noticeable difference in Anp1, Mnn9, Chs5, or Sec7 localization or the morphology of the Golgi compartments these proteins marked.
evidence: Supported by imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: No morphological difference for early- and medial-Golgi markers, Sed5 and Aur1, respectively, was observed for β′-COP ∆2–304 cells compared to WT cells.
source: Similarly, no morphological difference for early- and medial-Golgi markers, Sed5 and Aur1, respectively, was observed for β′-COP ∆2–304 cells compared to WT cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The total number of mNG-Gos1 or mNG-Bet1 fluorescent structures per optical section was not different between WT and β′-COP ∆2–304 cells.
source: No difference between WT and β′-COP ∆2–304 was observed for the total number of mNG-Gos1 or mNG-Bet1 fluorescent structures per optical section.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Relative to WT cells, a greater number of mNG-Gos1 and mNG-Bet1 structures were rings and tubes in the β′-COP ∆2–304 cells with a concomitant reduction in punctae.
source: However, relative to WT cells, a greater number of these structures were rings and tubes in the β′-COP ∆2–304 cells with a concomitant reduction in punctae.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: For the Golgi markers, the number of punctae per cell optical section was the same in WT and β′-COP ∆2–304 cells and the tube or ring structures were rarely observed.
source: For the Golgi markers, the number of punctae per cell optical section was the same in WT and mutant cells and the tube or ring structures were rarely observed.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The average size of intracellular structures was not significantly different for the Golgi markers in WT or β′-COP ∆2–304 cells.
source: The average size of intracellular structures was not significantly different for the Golgi markers in WT or β′-COP ∆2–304 cells (Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: For mNG-Gos1, the average length of the structures was significantly increased in β′-COP ∆2–304.
source: For mNG-Gos1, the average length of the structures was significantly increased in β′-COP ∆2–304.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The COPI mutation β′-COP ∆2–304 does not cause whole organelle-level changes in Golgi morphology or the localization of markers used in the study.
source: Thus, the COPI mutation used here does not cause whole organelle-level changes in Golgi morphology or the localization of markers used here (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 3).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantitative analysis data shown in Figure 2 and supplementary figures.

claim: Bet1 and Gos1 are substantially lost from Golgi compartments and mislocalized to tube- or ring-like structures in β′-COP ∆2–304 cells.
source: Bet1 and Gos1 are substantially lost from Golgi compartments and mislocalized to tube- or ring-like structures (Figures 1 and 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by imaging and colocalization analysis data shown in Figures 1 and 2 and supplementary figures.

claim: The majority of FM4-64-stained endosomes had a normal morphology in the β′-COP ∆2–304 mutant cells.
source: The majority of FM4-64-stained endosomes had a normal morphology in the mutant cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by FM4-64 staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: A subset of the mNG-SNARE tubular structures stain weakly with FM4-64.
source: We did see a subset of the mNG-SNARE tubular structures stain weakly with FM4-64.
evidence: Supported by FM4-64 staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The degree of colocalization between the SNAREs and FM4-64 as measured by the Mander's colocalization coefficient was not significantly different between WT and β′-COP ∆2–304 mutant cells.
source: However, the degree of colocalization between the SNAREs and FM4-64 as measured by the Mander's colocalization coefficient was not significantly different between WT and COPI mutant cells.
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Bet1 and Gos1 do not appear to be mislocalized from the Golgi to the endosomal system in the β′-COP ∆2–304 cells.
source: Therefore, it does not appear that Bet1 and Gos1 are being mislocalized from the Golgi to the endosomal system in the β′-COP ∆2–304 cells.
evidence: Inferred from the FM4-64 colocalization data showing no significant difference in colocalization between WT and mutant cells.

claim: No observable difference in the appearance or localization of Bet1 and Gos1 was observed in β′-COP-RKR cells compared to WT cells.
source: No observable difference in the appearance or localization of Bet1 and Gos1 was observed.
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3b.

claim: The ability of β′-COP to bind ubiquitin but not the dilysine motifs is critical for proper localization of SNAREs Bet1 and Gos1.
source: These observations suggest that the ability of β′-COP to bind ubiquitin but not the dilysine motifs is critical for proper localization of SNAREs Bet1 and Gos1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that β′-COP-RKR mutant, which cannot bind dilysine motifs, still supports normal Bet1 and Gos1 localization.

claim: The replacement of the β′-COP 2–304 domain with the general UBD, UBDDoa1 restored SNARE localization to punctate structures comparable to WT cells for Bet1, Gos1, and Snc1.
source: The replacement of the β′-COP 2–304 domain with the general UBD, UBDDoa1 restored SNARE localization to punctate structures comparable to WT cells (Figure 3a–f).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3a–f.

claim: β′-COP-UBDDoa1 does not restore the dilysine interaction.
source: β′-COP-UBDDoa1 does not restore the dilysine interaction (Xu et al., 2017); therefore, it is the ability of β′-COP to bind Ub that is critical for normal SNARE localization.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Xu et al., 2017).

claim: It is the ability of β′-COP to bind Ub that is critical for normal SNARE localization.
source: β′-COP-UBDDoa1 does not restore the dilysine interaction (Xu et al., 2017); therefore, it is the ability of β′-COP to bind Ub that is critical for normal SNARE localization.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that UBDDoa1 fusion, which cannot bind dilysine motifs but can bind ubiquitin, restores SNARE localization.

claim: The K63-linkage restricted β′-COP NZFTab2 construct did not significantly correct the Bet1 or Gos1 localization pattern.
source: Surprisingly, however, the K63-linkage restricted β′-COP NZFTab2 construct did not significantly correct the Bet1 or Gos1 localization pattern.
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3a, c, d, f.

claim: Both the UBDDoa1 and NZFTab2 constructs significantly restored the WT pattern of intracellular structures labeled with mNG-Snc1.
source: Consistently, we found here that both the UBDDoa1 and NZFTab2 constructs significantly restored the WT pattern of intracellular structures labeled with mNG-Snc1 (Figure 3b, e).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3b, e.

claim: UBDDoa1 restored the mNG-Snc2 WT pattern, but the K63-restricted NZFTab2 domain did not.
source: However, even though Snc2 is functionally and evolutionarily closely related to Snc1, we found that UBDDoa1 restored the mNG-Snc2 WT pattern, but the K63-restricted NZFTab2 domain did not (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: For GFP-Sec22, β′-COP-UBDDoa1 fully prevented vacuolar mislocalization while a partial rescue was conferred by β′-COP NZFTab2.
source: For GFP-Sec22, β′-COP-UBDDoa1 fully prevented vacuolar mislocalization while a partial rescue was conferred by β′-COP NZFTab2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c, d).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c, d.

claim: Snc1 and Sec22 can use K63-linked polyUb chains for their trafficking.
source: Thus, Snc1 and Sec22 can use K63-linked polyUb chains for their trafficking, but Bet1, Gos1, and Snc2 appear to rely on COPI binding to some other ubiquitin linkage type.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that NZFTab2 (K63-specific UBD) rescues Snc1 and partially rescues Sec22 but not Bet1, Gos1, or Snc2.

claim: Bet1, Gos1, and Snc2 appear to rely on COPI binding to some other ubiquitin linkage type besides K63.
source: Thus, Snc1 and Sec22 can use K63-linked polyUb chains for their trafficking, but Bet1, Gos1, and Snc2 appear to rely on COPI binding to some other ubiquitin linkage type.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that NZFTab2 (K63-specific UBD) does not rescue Bet1, Gos1, or Snc2 localization.

claim: Bet1, Snc1, and Snc2 were observed in tubular and ring-like structures in ret1-1 at the nonpermissive temperature.
source: Bet1, Snc1, and Snc2 were observed in tubular and ring-like structures in ret1-1 at the nonpermissive temperature (Figure 3a–f, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3a–f and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The localization pattern seen for Bet1, Snc1, and Snc2 in β′-COP Δ2–304 cells was comparable to ret1-1 at the nonpermissive temperature.
source: Interestingly, the localization pattern seen for Bet1, Snc1, and Snc2 in β′-COP Δ2–304 cells was comparable to ret1-1 at the nonpermissive temperature (Figure 1b–c; Figure 3a–c).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figures 1b–c and 3a–c.

claim: Perturbations in the ability of β′-COP to bind ubiquitin in β′-COP Δ2–304 substantially disrupt COPI function with respect to Bet1, Snc1, and Snc2 localization.
source: These data indicate that perturbations in the ability of β′-COP to bind ubiquitin in β′-COP Δ2–304 substantially disrupt COPI function with respect to Bet1, Snc1, and Snc2 localization.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the phenotype in β′-COP Δ2–304 is comparable to the ret1-1 COPI mutant at nonpermissive temperature.

claim: β′-COP has been shown to bind K63-polyUb chains but not K48-polyUb or monoubiquitin (monoUb).
source: β′-COP has been shown to bind K63-polyUb chains but not K48-polyUb or monoubiquitin (monoUb) (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Xu et al., 2017).

claim: β′-COP is capable of binding linear ubiquitin chains and more weakly to K6-, K11-, and K29-polyUb chains.
source: β′-COP is capable of binding linear ubiquitin chains and more weakly to K6-, K11-, and K29-polyUb chains (Figure 3g, h).
evidence: Supported by in vitro ubiquitin binding assay data shown in Figure 3g, h.

claim: Strains expressing COPI-DUB constructs, irrespective of whether α- or β′-COP was fused to DUB, were enlarged in size.
source: Strains expressing COPI-DUB constructs, irrespective of whether α- or β′-COP was fused to DUB, were enlarged in size (Figure 4a, b).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4a, b.

claim: Mislocalization of Bet1 and Gos1 was observed in COPI-DUB constructs wherein mNG-tagged SNAREs were observed in enlarged punctate structures, elongated tube structures, or ring-like structures.
source: Additionally, we observed mislocalization of Bet1 and Gos1 in COPI-DUB constructs wherein mNG-tagged SNAREs were observed in enlarged punctate structures, elongated tube structures, or ring-like structures (Figure 4a, c).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4a, c.

claim: COPI-DUB* constructs did not display significant phenotypic changes.
source: COPI-DUB* constructs did not display significant phenotypic changes.
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4a, c.

claim: The fusion of a DUB domain to COPI phenocopies the mislocalization pattern for Bet1 and Gos1 in the COPI (ret1-1) mutant at nonpermissive temperatures.
source: The fusion of a DUB domain to COPI phenocopies the mislocalization pattern for Bet1 and Gos1 in the COPI (ret1-1) mutant at nonpermissive temperatures, supporting the importance of ubiquitination in COPI-mediated regulation of SNARE localization.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that COPI-DUB constructs show similar mislocalization patterns as the ret1-1 mutant.

claim: Global analyses of the budding yeast proteome have identified ubiquitinated lysines in Gos1, Snc1, and Snc2 but not Bet1.
source: Global analyses of the budding yeast proteome have identified ubiquitinated lysines in Gos1, Snc1, and Snc2 but not Bet1 (Swaney et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Swaney et al., 2013).

claim: A smeared pattern associated with ubiquitination was observed for Gos1 in mock-treated samples, which collapsed, releasing a significant amount of monoUb following DUB treatment.
source: For Gos1-FLAG immunoprecipitations probed with antiubiquitin antibody, a smeared pattern was observed in the 50–80 kDa molecular weight region (Figure 5b) when probed with anti-Ub, which collapsed, releasing a significant amount of monoUb following DUB treatment (Figure 5c, d, Gos1 lanes).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5b, c, d.

claim: DUB treatment of Snc1 immunoprecipitates released more monoUb than control samples.
source: Although the smeared pattern for Snc1 was not apparent in these samples, DUB treatment released more monoUb than control samples (Figure 5d, Snc1).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Gos1 is reported to form a functional t-SNARE complex with Ykt6 and Sed5 that mediates fusion with intra-Golgi retrograde vesicles bearing Sft1.
source: Gos1 is reported to form a functional t-SNARE complex with Ykt6 and Sed5 that mediates fusion with intra-Golgi retrograde vesicles bearing Sft1 (Parlati et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Parlati et al., 2002).

claim: Significant enrichment of peptides from Ykt6, Sft1, and Sed5 with Gos1-FLAG was observed in SILAC MS analysis.
source: We observed significant enrichment of peptides from these partner SNAREs with Gos1-FLAG and known SNARE regulators like Sec17 and Sly1 (Demircioglu et al., 2014; Song et al., 2021; Figure 5e).
evidence: Supported by SILAC MS data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Several COPI subunit peptides were enriched to comparable levels as Ykt6, Sft1, and Sed5 in the Gos1 pulldown samples.
source: Importantly, we also found several COPI subunit peptides that were enriched to comparable levels as Ykt6, Sft1, and Sed5 in the Gos1 pulldown samples (Figure 5e).
evidence: Supported by SILAC MS data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: A smeared pattern associated with ubiquitination was observed for both Ykt6 and Sed5 in mock-treated samples, which was collapsed by DUB treatment to monoUb.
source: A smeared pattern associated with ubiquitination was observed for both Ykt6 (Figure 5f) and Sed5 (Figure 5h) in mock-treated samples, which was collapsed by DUB treatment to monoUb (Figure 5f–i).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5f–i.

claim: Gos1, Ykt6, and Sed5 are ubiquitinated.
source: These data support previously published high-throughput results indicating that Gos1, Ykt6, and Sed5 are ubiquitinated (Swaney et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in the manuscript and citation to prior work (Swaney et al., 2013).

claim: A substantial amount of monoUb was released from COPI and Glo3 immunoprecipitates following DUB treatment.
source: The FLAG IPs probed with antiubiquitin antibody show a substantial amount of monoUb released from COPI and Glo3 immunoprecipitates following the DUB treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a–e).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a–e.

claim: No significant change in the smeared electrophoretic pattern or the release of monoUb in the samples was observed with or without K48-specific DUB treatment.
source: No significant change in the smeared electrophoretic pattern or the release of monoUb in the samples was observed with or without K48-specific DUB treatment suggesting that the ubiquitination associated with COPI and Glo3 is not a degradation signal (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a-e).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a-e.

claim: The ubiquitination associated with COPI and Glo3 is not a degradation signal.
source: No significant change in the smeared electrophoretic pattern or the release of monoUb in the samples was observed with or without K48-specific DUB treatment suggesting that the ubiquitination associated with COPI and Glo3 is not a degradation signal (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a-e).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that K48-specific DUB treatment does not release ubiquitin from these complexes.

claim: No significant release of ubiquitin was observed following K63- or M1-DUB treatment of Gos1, Ykt6, Sed5, COPI, and Glo3 immunoprecipitates compared to the untagged control.
source: No significant release of ubiquitin was observed following K63- or M1-DUB treatment compared to the untagged control (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: A significant level of released ubiquitin was detected for Gos1, Ykt6, Sed5, COPI, and Glo3 samples when treated with the general deubiquitinase.
source: A significant level of released ubiquitin was detected for these samples when treated with the general deubiquitinase.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The lack of K63 linkages on COPI and SNARE components is consistent with live-cell imaging data showing that β′-COP with a K63-specific binding domain failed to support the trafficking of Bet1, Gos1, and Snc2.
source: The lack of K63 linkages on these components is also consistent with live-cell imaging data (Figure 3a–f), showing that β′-COP with a K63-specific binding domain failed to support the trafficking of Bet1, Gos1, and Snc2.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between biochemical data showing lack of K63 linkages and imaging data showing NZFTab2 does not rescue these SNAREs.

claim: The ubiquitination associated with Gos1, COPI, and Glo3 complexes appears to be nondegradative (non-K48 or non-K63) in nature.
source: Thus, the ubiquitination associated with Gos1, COPI, and Glo3 complexes appears to be nondegradative (non-K48 or non-K63) in nature and may modulate protein interactions in the COPI-dependent retrieval of SNAREs within the Golgi.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that K48- and K63-specific DUBs do not release ubiquitin from these complexes.

claim: Ubiquitination may modulate protein interactions in the COPI-dependent retrieval of SNAREs within the Golgi.
source: Thus, the ubiquitination associated with Gos1, COPI, and Glo3 complexes appears to be nondegradative (non-K48 or non-K63) in nature and may modulate protein interactions in the COPI-dependent retrieval of SNAREs within the Golgi.
evidence: Speculative statement about the potential role of ubiquitination based on the data.

claim: Significant enrichment of COPI subunits and Arf was observed with Gos1 when ubiquitination was preserved, compared to conditions where ubiquitin was removed.
source: Significant enrichment of COPI subunits and Arf was observed with Gos1 when ubiquitination was preserved, compared to 'w/o-ub' conditions (Figure 6e–g).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6e–g.

claim: Ubiquitination appears to play a role in the assembly and/or stability of COPI coatomer complex with Gos1.
source: The ubiquitination, thus, appears to play a role in the assembly and/or stability of COPI coatomer complex with Gos1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that COPI and Arf enrichment with Gos1 is enhanced when ubiquitination is preserved.

claim: COPI subunits are enriched with Bet1 under 'w Ub' conditions compared to 'w/o Ub'.
source: Nonetheless, we see the enrichment of COPI subunits with Bet1 under 'w Ub' conditions compared to 'w/o Ub' (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Arf is significantly enriched with Bet1 when ubiquitin was present on the complexes.
source: Similarly, Arf is significantly enriched with Bet1 when ubiquitin was present on the complexes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1e, f).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1e, f.

claim: The presence of DUB inhibitors during cell lysis was most critical to preserve the SNARE–COPI complex.
source: Control experiments indicated that the presence of DUB inhibitors during cell lysis was most critical to preserve the SNARE–COPI complex (Figure 6a, Figure 6—figure supplement 1g, h).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6a and Figure 6—figure supplement 1g, h.

claim: The role of ubiquitination in the assembly and stability of COPI coatomer complex with Bet1 appears to function independently of the Bet1 ubiquitination status.
source: Therefore, the role of ubiquitination in the assembly and stability of COPI coatomer complex with Bet1 appears to function independently of the Bet1 ubiquitination status.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Bet1 is not detectably ubiquitinated but still shows ubiquitin-dependent enrichment with COPI.

claim: Ubiquitin-mediated stabilization of COPI–Golgi SNARE complexes occurs.
source: Altogether, the data reveal ubiquitin-mediated stabilization of COPI–Golgi SNARE complexes.
evidence: Supported by the comparative pulldown data showing enhanced COPI-SNARE interactions when ubiquitination is preserved.

claim: A small amount of Glo3-GST coimmunoprecipitates with FLAG-Gos1, but no significant difference was observed in the presence or absence of Ub.
source: We detected a small amount of Glo3-GST coimmunoprecipitating with FLAG-Gos1, but no significant difference was observed in the presence or absence of Ub (Figure 7a, c).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7a, c.

claim: Association of Arf with Gos1 was significantly enriched using w Ub conditions compared to w/o-Ub conditions.
source: In contrast, association of Arf with Gos1 was significantly enriched using w Ub conditions compared to w/o-Ub conditions (Figure 7a, d).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7a, d.

claim: Glo3 was enriched with COPI in SILAC coimmunoprecipitation analysis using C-terminally FLAG-tagged α-COP under ubiquitin preserved conditions.
source: As expected, Glo3 was enriched with COPI, indicating eventual recruitment of Glo3 onto the COPI coat (Figure 7f).
evidence: Supported by SILAC MS data shown in Figure 7f.

claim: The COPI sample was enriched for several ER residence membrane proteins bearing C-terminal dilysine motifs.
source: The COPI sample was also enriched for several ER residence membrane proteins bearing C-terminal dilysine motifs (Figure 7f, red datapoints).
evidence: Supported by SILAC MS data shown in Figure 7f.

claim: No SNAREs were coimmunoprecipitated with COPI in the α-COP pulldown.
source: However, no SNAREs were coimmunoprecipitated with COPI, indicating that the COPI complexes recovered here were significantly different from SNARE–COPI complexes that contained Gos1.
evidence: Supported by SILAC MS data shown in Figure 7f.

claim: The COPI complexes recovered in the α-COP pulldown were significantly different from SNARE–COPI complexes that contained Gos1.
source: However, no SNAREs were coimmunoprecipitated with COPI, indicating that the COPI complexes recovered here were significantly different from SNARE–COPI complexes that contained Gos1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that α-COP pulldowns contain Glo3 and dilysine cargoes but not SNAREs, while Gos1 pulldowns contain SNAREs and COPI but not Glo3.

claim: No significant changes in the size or distribution of mNG-Gos1 punctae were observed in glo3Δ compared to WT cells.
source: Compared to WT cells, no significant changes in the size or distribution of mNG-Gos1 punctae were observed in glo3Δ (Figure 7g).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7g.

claim: Glo3 can weakly bind Gos1 but unlike COPI, this interaction is not stabilized by the presence of Ub.
source: Together, these data suggest that Glo3 can weakly bind Gos1 but unlike COPI, this interaction is not stabilized by the presence of Ub.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Glo3 coimmunoprecipitates with Gos1 at low levels and this is not enhanced by preserving ubiquitination.

claim: Glo3 does not appear to be required for COPI-dependent Gos1 localization.
source: In addition, Glo3 does not appear to be required for COPI-dependent Gos1 localization.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Gos1 localization is normal in glo3Δ cells.

claim: Ubiquitin plays critical role in stabilizing a complex between SNAREs, COPI, and Arf that is important for COPI function in retrieving a subset of SNAREs.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that ubiquitin plays critical role in stabilizing a complex between SNAREs, COPI, and Arf that is important for COPI function in retrieving a subset of SNAREs.
evidence: Supported by the collective data showing ubiquitin-dependent stabilization of SNARE-COPI-Arf complexes and the importance of COPI-ubiquitin interactions for SNARE localization.

claim: Glo3 appears to be present at low levels in the Gos1–Arf–COPI complex, but this interaction is not modulated by ubiquitination.
source: Glo3 appears to be present at low levels in the Gos1–Arf–COPI complex, but this interaction is not modulated by ubiquitination.
evidence: Supported by the data showing weak Glo3-Gos1 interaction that is not enhanced by preserving ubiquitination.

claim: The β′-COP ∆2–304 cells have substantially lost COPI function in sorting Bet1 and Gos1, which may underpin the slow growth phenotype of this mutant.
source: This suggests that the β′-COP ∆2–304 cells have substantially lost COPI function in sorting Bet1 and Gos1, which may underpin the slow growth phenotype of this mutant.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Bet1 and Gos1 mislocalization in β′-COP ∆2–304 is similar to the ret1-1 COPI mutant and the mutant has a slow growth phenotype.

claim: β′-COP-UBDDoa1 and β′-COP-RKR cells sort Gos1 and Bet1 normally and support WT growth of yeast.
source: In contrast, β′-COP-UBDDoa1 and β′-COP-RKR cells sort Gos1 and Bet1 normally, even though these β′-COP variants cannot bind to dilysine cargoes, and both variants support WT growth of yeast.
evidence: Supported by imaging data and growth phenotype observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The Gos1 and Bet1 phenotypes observed in β′-COP ∆2–304 are directly caused by a deficiency in β′-COP binding to polyUb and are not a secondary effect of disrupting the interaction with dilysine motifs.
source: Thus, the Gos1 and Bet1 phenotypes observed in β′-COP ∆2–304 are directly caused by a deficiency in β′-COP binding to polyUb and are not a secondary effect of disrupting the interaction with dilysine motifs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that β′-COP-RKR, which cannot bind dilysine motifs, still supports normal Gos1 and Bet1 localization.

claim: β′-COP binds preferentially to K63-linked polyUb chains and does not bind monoUb, diUb, or K48-linked polyUb chains.
source: β′-COP binds preferentially to K63-linked polyUb chains and does not bind monoUb, diUb, or K48-linked polyUb chains (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Xu et al., 2017).

claim: The replacement of the N-terminal WDR domain of β′-COP with the NZF domain from Tab2, which binds specifically to K63-linked polyUb, substantially restores Snc1 trafficking to the plasma membrane.
source: The replacement of the N-terminal WDR domain of β′-COP with the NZF domain from Tab2, which binds specifically to K63-linked polyUb, substantially restores Snc1 trafficking to the plasma membrane (Xu et al., 2017; Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Xu et al., 2017) and imaging data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The polyUb chains detected in the SNARE or COPI pulldowns are resistant to M1-, K63-, or K48-specific DUBs.
source: Moreover, the polyUb chains detected in the SNARE or COPI pulldowns are resistant to M1-, K63-, or K48-specific DUBs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The ubiquitin modifications present on COPI and SNARE components are unlikely to be targeting COPI to the proteasome or the SNAREs to the vacuole for degradation.
source: Thus, the ubiquitin modifications present are unlikely to be targeting COPI to the proteasome or the SNAREs to the vacuole for degradation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the ubiquitin chains are not K48- or K63-linked, which are typically associated with degradation.

claim: The nonproteolytic ubiquitin code regulates the COPI-dependent trafficking patterns for Golgi SNAREs.
source: Our data provide compelling evidence that the nonproteolytic ubiquitin code regulates the COPI-dependent trafficking patterns for Golgi SNAREs.
evidence: Supported by the collective data showing nondegradative ubiquitination regulates COPI-SNARE interactions and SNARE localization.

claim: PolyUb chains on SNAREs could form a sorting signal that COPI recognizes in order to recycle them from downstream compartments.
source: PolyUb chains on SNAREs could form a sorting signal that COPI recognizes in order to recycle them from downstream compartments, as previously proposed for Snc1 (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: Speculative statement based on prior work (Xu et al., 2017) and current data.

claim: It is possible that Bet1 associates with another cargo protein that is ubiquitinated, and the ubiquitin serves as the COPI-dependent sorting signal for both proteins.
source: It is possible that Bet1 associates with another cargo protein that is ubiquitinated, and the ubiquitin serves as the COPI-dependent sorting signal for both proteins.
evidence: Speculative statement to explain how Bet1, which is not detectably ubiquitinated, still depends on COPI-ubiquitin interactions.

claim: It is also possible that ubiquitination induces conformational changes in COPI driven by β′-COP interaction with ubiquitin attached to itself or to other COPI subunits.
source: It is also possible that ubiquitination induces conformational changes in COPI driven by β′-COP interaction with ubiquitin attached to itself or to other COPI subunits.
evidence: Speculative statement to explain how ubiquitination could affect COPI-SNARE interactions.

claim: Such a COPI conformational change could produce a high-affinity binding site for Bet1.
source: Such a COPI conformational change could produce a high-affinity binding site for Bet1.
evidence: Speculative statement to explain how ubiquitination could affect COPI-Bet1 interactions.

claim: The role of ubiquitin in mediating the stability of the COPI–SNARE complex is supported by the observation that Bet1 and Gos1 are mislocalized when ubiquitin is stripped from COPI–SNARE system by fusing a deubiquitinase domain to COPI components.
source: The role of ubiquitin in mediating the stability of the COPI–SNARE complex is further supported by the observation that Bet1 and Gos1 are mislocalized when ubiquitin is stripped from COPI–SNARE system by fusing a deubiquitinase domain to COPI components (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Cargo–coat interactions are typically low affinity.
source: We were surprised to find that COPI was co-enriched with Gos1-FLAG in the SILAC-based MS data (Figure 5e) because cargo–coat interactions are typically low affinity.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about cargo-coat interactions.

claim: Ubiquitination appears to regulate the assembly and/or stability of the COPI–cargo complex independent of the ubiquitination status of cargo.
source: Therefore, ubiquitination appears to regulate the assembly and/or stability of the COPI–cargo complex independent of the ubiquitination status of cargo.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Bet1, which is not detectably ubiquitinated, still shows ubiquitin-dependent enrichment with COPI.

claim: Not all ubiquitinated SNAREs relied on COPI–ubiquitin interaction for their sorting.
source: Not all ubiquitinated SNAREs relied on COPI–ubiquitin interaction for their sorting, For example, Sed5 is ubiquitinated but its localization is not affected by the alterations in the ability of COPI to recognize and bind ubiquitin (Figure 5h, i, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Sed5), and Sed5 appears to be independent of COPI for its Golgi localization (Gao and Banfield, 2020).
evidence: Supported by imaging data and citation to prior work (Gao and Banfield, 2020).

claim: Sed5 is ubiquitinated but its localization is not affected by the alterations in the ability of COPI to recognize and bind ubiquitin.
source: Not all ubiquitinated SNAREs relied on COPI–ubiquitin interaction for their sorting, For example, Sed5 is ubiquitinated but its localization is not affected by the alterations in the ability of COPI to recognize and bind ubiquitin (Figure 5h, i, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Sed5), and Sed5 appears to be independent of COPI for its Golgi localization (Gao and Banfield, 2020).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5h, i and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and citation to prior work (Gao and Banfield, 2020).

claim: Sed5 appears to be independent of COPI for its Golgi localization.
source: Not all ubiquitinated SNAREs relied on COPI–ubiquitin interaction for their sorting, For example, Sed5 is ubiquitinated but its localization is not affected by the alterations in the ability of COPI to recognize and bind ubiquitin (Figure 5h, i, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Sed5), and Sed5 appears to be independent of COPI for its Golgi localization (Gao and Banfield, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Gao and Banfield, 2020).

claim: A subset of Golgi SNAREs is dependent on the ability of COPI to bind ubiquitin.
source: A subset of Golgi SNAREs is dependent on the ability of COPI to bind ubiquitin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), and it is likely that other ubiquitin-independent interactions contribute to cargo selection.
evidence: Supported by the collective data showing that some SNAREs depend on COPI-ubiquitin interactions while others do not.

claim: It is likely that other ubiquitin-independent interactions contribute to cargo selection.
source: A subset of Golgi SNAREs is dependent on the ability of COPI to bind ubiquitin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), and it is likely that other ubiquitin-independent interactions contribute to cargo selection.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the observation that not all COPI cargoes depend on ubiquitin interactions.

claim: Cells are viable when all dilysine-binding sites in COPI are mutated.
source: α and β′COP WDR domains are required for the sorting of dilysine motif COPI cargoes, but cells are viable when all dilysine-binding sites are mutated (Jackson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Jackson et al., 2012).

claim: Ubiquitin binding by COPI WDR domains contributes to the essential function of COPI.
source: Our data suggest that ubiquitin binding by these COPI WDR domains contributes to the essential function of COPI because yeast harboring β′COP-UBDDoa1 grow much better than strains harboring β′COP-∆2–304 (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that replacing the WDR domain with a UBD rescues the growth defect of β′COP-∆2–304.

claim: The human β′COP-β-propeller binds polyUb and can function in yeast to support the normal localization of mNG-Snc1.
source: We have previously shown that the human β′COP-β-propeller also binds polyUb and can function in yeast to support the normal localization of mNG-Snc1, suggesting that the COPI–ubiquitin interaction is functionally conserved.
evidence: Supported by prior work from the authors.

claim: The COPI–ubiquitin interaction is functionally conserved.
source: We have previously shown that the human β′COP-β-propeller also binds polyUb and can function in yeast to support the normal localization of mNG-Snc1, suggesting that the COPI–ubiquitin interaction is functionally conserved.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that human β′COP can functionally replace yeast β′COP in ubiquitin-dependent SNARE trafficking.

claim: SNAREs are thought to prime coat assembly through interactions with Arf, ArfGAPs, and COPI as a mechanism to ensure vesicles form with an adequate load of v-SNAREs.
source: SNAREs are thought to prime coat assembly through interactions with Arf, ArfGAPs, and COPI as a mechanism to ensure vesicles form with an adequate load of v-SNAREs (Rein et al., 2002; Spang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Rein et al., 2002; Spang et al., 2010).

claim: The ArfGAP Glo3 contains a BoCCS motif that mediates binding to both COPI and to several different SNAREs.
source: The ArfGAP Glo3 contains a BoCCS motif that mediates binding to both COPI and to several different SNAREs, suggesting that Glo3 is a key determinant of the priming complex (Schindler and Spang, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Schindler and Spang, 2007).

claim: Glo3 is proposed to be a key determinant of the priming complex.
source: The ArfGAP Glo3 contains a BoCCS motif that mediates binding to both COPI and to several different SNAREs, suggesting that Glo3 is a key determinant of the priming complex (Schindler and Spang, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Schindler and Spang, 2007).

claim: It is unclear how Glo3 could facilitate coat assembly when its enzymatic function is to inactivate Arf.
source: However, it is unclear how Glo3 could facilitate coat assembly when its enzymatic function is to inactivate Arf.
evidence: Based on the known function of ArfGAPs and the proposed role of Glo3 in priming.

claim: The SNARE/Arf-GTP/COPI priming complex is stabilized by ubiquitination of the components and is devoid of ArfGAP.
source: Therefore, we suggest that the SNARE/Arf-GTP/COPI priming complex is stabilized by ubiquitination of the components and is devoid of ArfGAP.
evidence: Inferred from the data showing ubiquitin-stabilized SNARE-COPI-Arf complexes lack Glo3.

claim: Arf-GDP and COPI likely dissociate rapidly from the complex as the ArfGAP binds.
source: Arf-GDP and COPI likely dissociate rapidly from the complex as the ArfGAP binds (Figure 7h).
evidence: Speculative statement based on the model proposed in Figure 7h.

claim: Cycles of ubiquitination and deubiquitination could control the switch from Arf-GTP/SNARE-mediated assembly of COPI during budding and ArfGAP-mediated disassembly and uncoating of vesicles prior to fusion.
source: Ubiquitin-dependent enrichment of Arf and COPI with SNAREs suggests that cycles of ubiquitination and deubiquitination could control the switch from Arf-GTP/SNARE-mediated assembly of COPI during budding and ArfGAP-mediated disassembly and uncoating of vesicles prior to fusion.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the data showing ubiquitin-dependent stabilization of SNARE-COPI-Arf complexes.

claim: Ubiquitination–deubiquitination cycles for key components within the COPI-SNARE system may alter the coatomer assembly–disassembly dynamics regulating COPI function.
source: Ubiquitination–deubiquitination cycles for key components within the COPI-SNARE system thus may alter the coatomer assembly–disassembly dynamics regulating COPI function.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the data showing ubiquitin-dependent regulation of COPI-SNARE interactions.
